item.title: The 'developed country' label is actually a trap: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 00:30:00
A busy scene at the Port of Shanghai on July 24, 2026 Photo: VCG The international discussions on the positioning of China's development are an acknowledgment of China's developmental achievements and its responsibilities as a major power. However, we must be vigilant against certain narratives that deliberately obscure China's developmental stage, impose obligations that exceed its current phase of development, constrict China's developmental space, and create rifts between China and other developing countries, therefore putting China in a difficult position. The Wall Street Journal recently published an article saying that China is on the cusp of becoming a high-income country by the World Bank's classification. "China doesn't want to join the ranks of the world's developed countries," the article claimed, arguing that China benefits from its current status in international groups as "developing." In fact, being a high-income country is not the same as being a developed country. By conflating the two concepts, the Wall Street Journal article attempts to exert public pressure on China to shoulder international obligations that go beyond its current level of development. According to World Bank estimates, China's gross national income (GNI) per capita stood at $14,230 in 2025, slightly below the high-income threshold of $14,375. It is worth noting that this World Bank classification is based solely on GNI per capita, rather than a comprehensive assessment of a country's level of modernization, industrial development and public services. In recent years, countries such as Chile, Uruguay, Panama and Costa Rica have crossed the World Bank's high-income threshold. However, they are still widely regarded by the international community as developing countries or emerging economies, rather than automatically being classified as developed countries simply because they have reached the high-income threshold. As Chinese modernization steadily advances, China has made historic achievements in economic and social development, with its GDP firmly ranking second in the world. However, multiple indicators show that China's status as a developing country remains unchanged. For example, there is still a significant gap in per capita GDP compared to developed economies like those in Europe and the US, regional development imbalances have not yet been fundamentally resolved, and disparities persist between urban and rural areas. By contrast, the development process of Western developed countries is a comprehensive state formed after highly mature industrialization, urbanization, and modernization. This is reflected not only in the scale of their economies but also in various dimensions such as per capita wealth, social security systems, public service capacity, and scientific and technological innovation systems. The international discussions on the positioning of China's development largely stem from the rapid pace of China's growth and its significant contributions to the global economy, which have long surpassed the conventional narrative framework for traditional developing countries. These discussions are an acknowledgment of China's developmental achievements and its responsibilities as a major power. However, we must be vigilant against certain narratives that deliberately obscure China's developmental stage, impose obligations that exceed its current phase of development, constrict China's developmental space, and create rifts between China and other developing countries, therefore putting China in a difficult position. For China, its status as a developing country carries special political significance. China has always been a member of the Global South. This "South" is not merely a geographical or economic concept but an identity formed by emerging market countries and developing nations based on similar historical circumstances, current stages of development, common developmental goals, and shared political aspirations. Those who are eager to label China as a "developed country" are not truly seeking China's "graduation," but rather its "exclusion," aiming to detach China from the Global South camp. In this regard, China is very clear-minded and will not fall into this trap. To assess a country's international responsibilities, one should not only consider whether it has been labeled a "developed country," but rather whether it is genuinely promoting global common development. China's average annual contribution to global economic growth has long been around 30 percent. China is the largest contributor of peacekeeping personnel among the permanent members of the UN Security Council, and its four global initiatives offer Chinese wisdom,solutions and strength for global governance. China's contributions to building an open, inclusive, clean and beautiful world that enjoys lasting peace, common security, and common prosperity have already surpassed those of many developed countries. However, China will always be a member of the developing world; this is not modesty, but a reflection of sobriety and a sense of responsibility.

item.title: China, EU hybrid auto trade deal secures export growth, fair treatment for Chinese firms: observers
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 23:32:00
China EU Photo:VCG China and the EU held more than 30 rounds of intensive consultations on hybrid and electric vehicle (EV) trade, during which the Chinese negotiating team maintained an open attitude and kept up dialogue with the automotive industries on both sides, a source familiar with the talks told the Global Times. The two sides reached an arrangement for upward adjustment based on the EU's 2025 imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles, with a fixed annual increase thereafter, ensuring room for Chinese automakers to maintain and steadily expand their exports, according to China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) on Monday. They also agreed that no measures would specifically target Chinese products or discriminate against Chinese companies, and that China's quota would be no lower than that granted to any other source of EU imports. The arrangement was among 16 outcomes reached during the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation (TIC) mechanism in Beijing on October 8 and 9, covering issues including trade and investment, export controls, intellectual property rights and World Trade Organization (WTO) reform. The hybrid vehicle arrangement has drawn attention following foreign media reports suggesting that it could cut China's hybrid vehicle exports to the EU by more than half over the next four years compared with projected levels. The Global Times learned that the negotiations were based on the EU's actual imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles in 2025. According to Eurostat data, the EU imported 107,000 hybrid vehicles from China in 2024, rising to 302,000 in 2025. Under the rules governing safeguard investigations, calculations must be based on the importing economy's official statistics, Chen Jingjing, secretary-general of the automotive branch of the China Chamber of Commerce for Import and Export of Machinery and Electronic Products, told the Global Times. "By securing an arrangement that allows exports to continue growing from the EU's actual 2025 import level, China has secured the greatest possible export benefits for its automakers," she said. Analysts noted that the claim of a more than 50 percent reduction was based on projecting the rapid growth of Chinese hybrid vehicle exports in recent years over the next four years and comparing the resulting figures with the negotiated arrangement, rather than the actual import volumes used in the talks. Such projections are inherently uncertain, given the influence of short-term market factors on past export growth. Notably, the arrangement applies only to hybrid passenger cars, rather than all Chinese vehicle exports to the EU. Chinese customs data showed that China exported about 1.009 million vehicles to the bloc in 2025, up 30.4 percent year-on-year, including 181,000 fuel-powered vehicles, 472,000 electric vehicles and 356,000 hybrids. Hybrids accounted for about 35.3 percent of the total, or roughly one-third, showing that the arrangement covers only a portion of China's automotive exports to the EU. Zhou Mi, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times that the arrangement addresses the concerns of industries on both sides while preserving room for continued export growth and business planning. The EU has substantial demand for imported vehicles, particularly hybrids, and restricting imports from China would make that demand more difficult to meet, he said. Over the past several decades, Chinese companies have strengthened their capabilities through fair competition, innovation and responding to customer needs, Zhou said. Equal treatment would therefore provide a stronger foundation for companies to pursue cooperation, he added. The recent consultations helped stabilize broader business expectations. Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao said during a meeting with Danone CEO Antoine de Saint-Affrique on Monday that the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism had produced a series of outcomes and understandings that helped stabilize industry expectations. Wang also said that China remains committed to expanding high-standard opening-up, with its growing consumer market and continued consumption upgrading creating broad opportunities for foreign-invested enterprises. He welcomed Danone to expand its investment and innovation-driven research and development in China. The broader significance of China-EU trade negotiations ultimately lies in whether they can give businesses on both sides the confidence to invest and operate in stable and predictable market conditions, analysts said. However, while China approached the negotiations with sincerity, some actions by the EU undermined mutual trust, according to the source. China has demonstrated both sincerity and patience in seeking negotiated solutions, but sincerity cannot be one-sided, nor is China's patience without limits. Against this backdrop, the two sides' confirmation that trade arrangements must comply with WTO rules is particularly important. Chen said that this means China retains all its rights under the WTO framework, including the right to seek dispute settlement and trade compensation. If the EU violates relevant WTO rules during its investigation, China can use all lawful means consistent with those rules to effectively safeguard the interests of Chinese enterprises, providing greater reassurance to businesses, Chen said.

item.title: Global experts hail China's Pinglu Canal, praise remarkable engineering, ecological achievements
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 22:48:00
A vessel sails along the Pinglu Canal near the Madao hub. Photo: Courtesy of Pinglu Canal Group The newly opened Pinglu Canal in South China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region has become a focal point of discussion for industry experts from home and abroad at the ongoing World Canals Conference 2026 (WCC) in Guilin, Guangxi, as many hailed the canal's economic value, engineering feats and ecological contribution. The conference runs from Monday to Friday in Guilin. Notably, this year's event closely follows the recent opening of the Pinglu Canal, which is also located in the autonomous region in South China. The 134.2-kilometer Pinglu Canal is the first canal planned and coordinated at the national level since 1949 to connect a river to the sea, and it opens up the shortest, most economical, and most convenient sea outlet for southwestern China. It is a backbone project of the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor that connects with the China-proposed Belt and Road Initiative and marks a major addition to the nation's river network. The project has set four world records among comparable canals: the highest navigation capacity, the fastest ship-lock transit speed, the highest lift for a water-saving ship lock, and the largest water-saving ship lock on an inland waterway. As hundreds of canal experts from home and abroad gathered in Guilin, the Pinglu Canal's engineering achievements as well as other features such as ecological protection, were constantly acknowledged by participants in the event. "There is something quite remarkable about witnessing the beginning of an entirely new canal corridor," Sharon Leighton, president of Inland Waterways International, said at the opening ceremony of the event on Tuesday. "The Pinglu Canal introduces a new chapter in the long story of populations using waterways to connect and create opportunity." "Of everything I know, this is remarkable and leading," Leighton told the Global Times on Monday, commenting on the canal's engineering achievements in solving technical difficulties. Tomas Kolark, a canal expert from the Czech Republic, told the Global Times that the Pinglu Canal is very impressive in terms of engineering and water management. "I was watching closely the preparations and mainly the construction of the canal, and it was very interesting to see it now with my own eyes," Kolark said. "Another interesting approach of the canal was, for example, it is maybe one of the world's first bridges for wildlife crossings." As a project built with protecting the environment and ecology in mind, the Pinglu Canal has built fish passages, animal bridges and bird corridors, reflecting a deliberate effort to harmonize infrastructure with nature, the Global Times learned from Pinglu Canal Group, the builder of the canal. "It was interesting to see that 98 percent of the material excavated from the canal's construction was used for construction purposes. In all, it's very interesting to see how the canal was planned and built, and we could see today how it's used," said Kolark. Eddie Lee, a participant in the event, told the Global Times that she learned through visits to some of the hubs along the Pinglu Canal, where she saw how engineers tackled the difficulties in managing the high-water lift. She also understood the special technology used on the ship lock's gates to ensure smooth opening and closing while withstanding the high pressure. "It's interesting to know that Chinese engineers have worked with academia and top technology universities to tackle the issues," Lee said. "I understand that it will be very important for the economy in Guangxi, in [Southwest China's] Guizhou Province, and in [Southwest China's] Yunnan Province. I have traveled a lot in China, seeing that some southern parts have not developed as fast as northern or eastern parts. I think the Pinglu Canal will make a big difference." For its achievement, the Pinglu Canal Project was awarded the Green Design International Award by the World Green Design Organization on Tuesday, according to the Beijing-based stdaily.com.

item.title: GT Voice: What Paris Motor Show signals about China-Europe auto co-op
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 22:09:00
The Paris Motor Show runs October 12-18, 2026 in Paris, France. Photo: VCG The biennial Paris Motor Show officially kicked off on Monday, with a record number of Chinese automakers taking part to showcase their latest models and technologies. A total of 25 Chinese brands, represented by 16 companies, including BYD, XPeng, Changan, Dongfeng and Leapmotor, are taking part, roughly double the number at the 2024 edition. Such a scale of participation from Chinese carmakers would have been almost unimaginable a decade ago, yet it is now very much a real scene in the exhibition halls of the Paris Motor Show. Behind this lies the rapid rise of Chinese automakers globally. The Paris show has long served as a reliable barometer of the global auto industry, and this year's edition sent an unmistakable signal: China-Europe electric vehicle (EV) cooperation is moving from simple trade to deeper industrial integration. Compared with the previous show, Chinese brands' recognition, user base and market foothold in Europe have grown noticeably, and their development path has gradually shifted from pure vehicle exports toward deep localization, with production bases, research and development (R&D) centers, distribution networks and after-sales systems being established across Europe. For a long time, some in Europe have viewed Chinese carmakers through a zero-sum lens, framing normal market competition as a "shock" to local industries. This year's Paris Motor Show, however, makes clear that framing such cooperation simply as a threat no longer holds against the increasingly diverse and pragmatic reality in China-Europe cooperation. Chinese carmakers are using flexible approaches such as joint plant construction and joint development to revitalize existing local capacity, drive employment and supply chains, and offer European consumers more cost-effective models. This model is not zero-sum but complementary. For instance, Stellantis and China's Leapmotor announced plans in May to start joint car production in Europe, with two models to be built in Spain, deepening their tie-up beyond distribution into manufacturing. This is a win-win arrangement, as European companies need such cooperation to raise productivity, while Chinese automakers need a localized foundation to take root in the market. Europe's vehicle industry stands at a critical stage of electrification, and Chinese carmakers' strengths in batteries, electronic controls and intelligent systems align neatly with Europe's robust manufacturing base and brand heritage. Joint plants shorten construction cycles and reduce policy risk, while joint development shares R&D costs and speeds up product iteration. This is not one side swallowing the other, but making the cake bigger together. An increasing number of European industry bodies, local partners and ordinary consumers are recognizing the real value of this cooperation. The jobs created, technology spillovers and industrial increments brought by Chinese brands cannot be overlooked. For example, BYD plans to expand its European workforce to more than 40,000 people by 2030, a target that would place the Chinese carmaker among the largest non-European automotive employers in the region, according to Bloomberg. This tangible market dividend is far more persuasive than any protectionist slogan. From a broader perspective, the deepening of China-Europe EV cooperation is also a microcosm of the transformation of the global car industry. For decades, the division of labor in the global automotive sector remained relatively fixed, and China was long a latecomer playing catch-up. But in the wave of electrification and intelligence, China has built distinct advantages in batteries and intelligent driving, while Europe retains profound accumulated strengths in traditional areas. Cooperation is a two-way journey where each side brings its own strengths to jointly define new products. Recognizing these new signals of cooperation does not mean the road ahead is smooth. China-Europe EV cooperation still faces multiple challenges, from geopolitical noise to protectionism. Chinese automakers need to adapt to changing market trends in Europe. Europe, for its part, must let reason overcome prejudice, respect facts, and treat Chinese carmakers fairly in line with WTO rules. The Paris Motor Show this time may be witnessing the arrival of a new era of industrial collaboration: the automotive industries of China and Europe can make the cake bigger through open cooperation and forge a path that benefits industry, companies and consumers alike.

item.title: Will the Pinglu Canal widen ASEAN's trade deficit with China?: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 21:40:00
A vessel sails along the Pinglu Canal near the Madao hub. Photo: Courtesy of Pinglu Canal Group Editor's Note: Currently, China's economy is steadily advancing along the path of high-quality development, even as domestic and international circumstances become increasingly complex. Some Western media, due to misunderstanding or bias, have repeatedly questioned or even distorted China's economic development. Accordingly, the Global Times launches the "Q&A on China's Economy" column to publish opinion pieces to present facts and clarify perceptions. The Pinglu Canal has been operational since September 16. As the latest landmark project in China-ASEAN connectivity, the canal is a public good serving the wider region. However, since construction of the canal began, there have been noises in the West and certain ASEAN countries arguing that lower logistics costs could "flood" ASEAN markets with more Chinese goods, leading to trade "imbalance" between China and ASEAN and posing challenges for the development of local industries in Southeast Asia. Such concerns are based to some extent on the realities of regional trade and economic relations, but the logic behind them is overly simplistic. As is well known, China and ASEAN have remained each other's largest trading partners since 2020. Their industrial chains are deeply interconnected, with intermediate goods accounting for more than 60 percent of bilateral trade. At the same time, many ASEAN economies maintain large trade surpluses with the US and Europe while running trade deficits with China. Will the opening of the Pinglu Canal therefore widen ASEAN countries' trade deficits with China? Such a view is clearly one-sided, for two reasons. First, the current China-ASEAN trade pattern is determined by the regional division of labor in industrial and supply chains, not by the Pinglu Canal. The existing pattern of bilateral trade between China and ASEAN countries does not exist in isolation. It forms part of a triangular division of labor that has developed over time in the region and within global industrial chains. The opening of the canal will not change regional comparative advantages, nor will it create trade imbalances. One important fact should not be overlooked. Many ASEAN countries run trade surpluses with European and US markets, and these surpluses often rely on intermediate goods, components, machinery and equipment imported from China. ASEAN countries process and assemble raw materials and components imported from China, and then export the finished products to end markets in Europe and the US. As a result, some ASEAN countries run trade deficits with China while maintaining surpluses with Europe and the US. This stems from the current regional industrial division of labour. The logistical convenience brought by the canal helps ASEAN countries leverage regional supply chains to expand exports to third-party markets, generating mutually beneficial outcomes at the level of regional industrial chains. Second, as a public good for regional connectivity, the Pinglu Canal serves as a low-cost waterway that is open to market participants on both sides. It is not designed only to serve Chinese exporters. It can transport Chinese goods southward while also facilitating the movement of ASEAN agricultural products, minerals, forest products and components northward into China's vast inland consumer and production markets, and even onward to the broader Eurasian market. Currently, China's month-on-month year-over-year import growth rate has outpaced export growth for six consecutive months. China's catalytic role in regional and even global trade and the economy has become more pronounced. Against this backdrop, the Pinglu Canal will help China import more ASEAN products in the years ahead. The structure of industrial chains is not fixed. ASEAN countries are promoting industrial upgrading, and their capacity to export higher value-added products continues to grow. Amid elevated global energy prices, international freight rates and inflation, which have pushed up regional firms' costs and squeezed their profit margins, the low-cost transport route provided by the Pinglu Canal comes at an opportune moment, acting as a booster for ASEAN's manufacturing upgrade and facilitating easier access for locally manufactured products to China's inland markets. The opening of the Pinglu Canal will, in the long term, strengthen China-ASEAN trade and the resilience of regional industrial and supply chains. As ASEAN goods enter China's inland markets at lower logistics costs, ASEAN economies will also become more deeply integrated into industrial chains in China. ASEAN products, from agricultural goods such as fruit, rice, rubber and palm oil to resources such as bauxite, will be able to move beyond China's coastal markets and reach more deeply into its western inland regions. At the same time, the canal will make central and western China more open to ASEAN and can also promote the development and transformation of Chinese industries. The benefits of lower logistics costs brought by the Pinglu Canal can only be realized through joint efforts. Take the second ship lock on Xijin reservoir, regarded as a key gateway to the canal, as an example. It has handled a cumulative cargo volume of 70.8 million tons over the past three years. Realizing the canal's full potential requires China and ASEAN countries to jointly build and make good use of two-way logistics chains. As ASEAN goods gain lower-cost access to markets in Southwest China, enterprises, ports and logistics service providers along the route will all play important roles in shaping the emerging canal economy. In short, the so-called "one-way corridor" narrative is essentially a new variant of the "China squeeze" narrative. The mutually beneficial and win-win cooperation framework between China and ASEAN remains unchanged, and will stay so. Only by expanding the pie of regional cooperation can China, ASEAN and more countries secure larger slices for themselves. In this process, the Pinglu Canal will serve not only as a multiplier for the expansion and optimization of trade, but also as a catalyst for structural improvement.

item.title: Police probes man for doing pull-ups on beam at 1,500-y-o historic Hanging Temple in North China's Shanxi
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 21:05:00
Photo: Screenshot from CCTV A video of a man doing pull-ups on a beam at the 1,500-year-old Xuankong Temple, or Hanging Temple, in Datong, North China’s Shanxi Province, has gone viral recently, sparking public concerns about potential damage to the historic structure, China Central Television (CCTV) reported on Tuesday. The Hengshan Mountain Scenic Spot Management Center responded on Tuesday that the public security authorities have launched an investigation. According to a statement released by the management center, surveillance footage confirmed that the incident occurred on September 27 at the Mahavira Hall of the Hanging Temple. The individual involved uploaded the video to social media on October 11, triggering widespread public attention the next day. Upon learning of the incident, ancient architecture and heritage conservation experts were dispatched to conduct an on-site inspection. A professional inspection confirmed that the behavior had not caused any visible direct physical damage to the heritage structure at this stage. However, given that the temple is a cliff side structure built entirely of wood, with its beams, crossbeams and columns interlocked through traditional mortise-and-tenon structure to distribute loads, such hanging and pulling activities pose a potential risk of disturbing the structural balance of the wooden framework, creating a serious safety hazard, the statement said. First built during the Northern Wei Dynasty (386-534), the Hanging Temple is a nationally protected cultural heritage site and a rare cliff side wooden complex that house Buddhist, Taoist and Confucian shrines. Featuring an ingenious architectural design, the temple relies on crossbeams embedded in the cliff for structural support. Any abnormal force on its load-bearing components could disrupt its centuries-old structural balance and cause irreversible damage, the statement said. Therefore, stepping on, pulling, shaking or climbing on the temple’s structural components is strictly prohibited, as doing so violates both the scenic area management rules and legal protections for cultural heritage, the statement added. After the video sparked controversy, the police formally opened an investigation and said they will deal with the individual in accordance with the law, the statement said. Next, the scenic area will step up patrols in key areas, install more warning signs and strengthen on-site visitor management to better protect the cultural heritage site, according to the statement. item.title: Philippine VP defends herself, saying Marcos' attacks threaten national security, ties with China
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 20:25:00
Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte Photo: VCG Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte said on Monday that recent remarks by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr pose threats to the Philippines' national security, China-Philippines ties, and regional stability, after Marcos linked the vice president to "funding from China," amid the recent impeachment trial against Duterte. A Chinese expert warned that weaponizing bilateral ties with China for domestic political gains is a short-sighted gambit destined to backfire. It may also further drive the Philippines away from the mainstream of ASEAN-China cooperation and into deeper self-isolation. According to media outlet Philstar.com, Marcos on Sunday claimed that it could be a national security threat "at the highest level" if the company linked to Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio did receive funds from China. Marcos' remarks come as Duterte is facing impeachment proceedings. On Tuesday, the Philippine prosecution panel informed the Senate impeachment court that it was dropping three of the four charges against Duterte, retaining only the allegation of unexplained wealth. In response to Marcos' latest accusation, Duterte said in a Monday statement issued by the Office of the Vice President of Philippines on Facebook that the Marcos administration is using "all its power, including intelligence agencies and law enforcement agencies" to suppress and undermine her. "Marcos' statement clearly states that for him, doing business with China is a threat to the security of the Philippines. This carries the connotation of a warning to Filipino businessmen doing business in China," she said. She also described Marcos' remarks as a bold and dangerous challenge to China, as it is accusing China of interfering in the internal affairs of the Philippines that lacks sufficient justification. "This is serious. And it could have a serious impact on our relationship with China," she added, the media reported. Chen Xiangmiao, a researcher at the National Institute for South China Sea Studies, told the Global Times that Marcos' move aims to label Duterte, who holds relatively pragmatic stances, as "pro-China" to court support from the country's right-wing and pro-US blocs and consolidate his political base. Chen added that a sitting president personally smearing China amid domestic factional infighting undermines the dignity and stature befitting a head of state, and reflects the Philippines' increasingly radical China policy. Defending Duterte, her spokesperson Paolo Panelo said on Monday that the Philippines cannot demonize Beijing for political propaganda, maintaining that relations with China should not be driven by political attacks, according to NewsWatch Plus PH. Hyping China-related issues to harvest domestic political gains has become a path dependency for some Philippine politicians, Chen said. "This practice inflicts severe damage on bilateral ties. Such short-sighted, high-risk political opportunism will inevitably come with a price," Chen noted. Politically, it will continue to poison the bilateral atmosphere, stoke public antagonism between the two peoples, marginalize moderate voices, erode the popular foundation of bilateral ties and substantially raise the cost for future Philippine administrations to reset relations, Chen said. Economically, China-related tourism, goods, trade, investment, infrastructure and livelihood projects in the Philippines may face disruptions or even suspension, Chen noted. "In the long run, Philippines' energy security, industrial upgrading, agricultural modernization, new-energy transition and digital economy may suffer spillover damage for its China policy… The risks incurred will ultimately be borne by Filipino people and succeeding administrations." In the Facebook statement, Duterte said that Marcos' remarks were intended to divert attention from what she described as his failure to properly address the territorial dispute between the Philippines and China. She warned that the issue could have implications beyond the Philippines, potentially affecting security and stability in the ASEAN region. Echoing Duterte, Anna Malindog-Uy, a columnist with The Manila Times, criticized the Marcos government in an X post on Tuesday, saying that the Philippines is playing an increasingly disruptive role in Southeast Asia under the current administration. "While many ASEAN countries pursue pragmatic diplomacy, economic cooperation, and strategic balance in their relations with China, the Marcos administration appears determined to turn the Philippines into the frontline of Washington's geopolitical confrontation with Beijing," she wrote. As China's comprehensive national strength and regional influence grow, ASEAN states see great potential in working with China, forming tightly linked industrial networks covering infrastructure, AI, digital economy, green sectors and cross-border trade, Chen said. "Against this backdrop, Manila's persistent tilt toward the US increases the risk of decoupling from ASEAN's China cooperation trend and self-isolation, and has become a regional destabilizer," said Chen, adding that weaponizing bilateral ties with China for domestic political gain is a short-sighted gambit destined to backfire.

item.title: Chinese courts sentence three Myanmar-based Wei family crime group members to death, demonstrating extraterritorial application of China's criminal law: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 19:33:00
Photo: from People's Daily A Chinese court on Tuesday sentenced three members of the Myanmar-based Wei family criminal group to death in first-instance verdicts. Three others received life imprisonment, while 55 defendants were sentenced to prison terms ranging from three years and 3 months to 24 years. The Intermediate People's Court of Quanzhou and people's court of Nan'an, both in East China's Fujian Province, publicly announced their first-instance verdicts in a series of cases involving the Wei family criminal group on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, according to media reports. Wei Huairen, Chen Dawei and Liao Jingfang were sentenced to death, while Wei Qingtao, Kang Min and Xiong Hengxing were sentenced to life imprisonment. The other 55 defendants, including Su Hongxiang, Deng Zida and Chen Longjiang, received fixed-term prison sentences, along with additional penalties including fines, confiscation of property and deportation, as applicable. The courts found that since 2019, two criminal groups had exploited the Wei family's influence in the Kokang region of Myanmar to establish multiple criminal compounds in Laukkaing and provide armed protection for crime bosses operating there. The one group, led by Wei Huairen and Wei Qingsong, who is being handled in a separate case, included Chen Longjiang, a close subordinate, and armed force leaders Cha Guicheng and Yan Longdi, both of whom are also being handled in separate cases, among its key members. The other group, known as the Henry criminal group, was led by Wei Rong, Wei Qinghai, both of whom are being handled in separate cases, and Wei Qingtao. Its key members included family member Su Hongxiang and close subordinate Deng Zida. The groups relied on armed forces controlled by the Wei family to provide armed protection for multiple crime bosses who set up operations in the compounds. They independently or jointly with these operators committed a range of crimes, including telecom and online fraud, operating casinos, extortion, organizing prostitution, drug trafficking and organizing others to illegally cross national borders. The two groups were involved in gambling- and fraud-related funds totaling more than 12.2 billion yuan ($1.7 billion), according to the court findings. The Wei family criminal group also colluded with telecom fraud gangs operating in the compounds to kill people involved in fraud who refused to comply with their orders, resulting in the deaths of two Chinese citizens. In addition, Chen Dawei, a member of the Wei family, used armed forces under his control to kill people indiscriminately, causing the deaths of another two Chinese citizens. According to the documentary The Demise of Myanmar-Based Telecom Fraud, which offers a rare look into the brutal reality of Myanmar-based cyber-scam networks and China's crackdown on cross-border telecom fraud, Chen was asked how he felt when he pledged brotherhood with others and killed people in a ritual sacrifice to heaven. "Was there anything to feel? I felt nothing," Chen replied. The courts ruled that defendants including Wei Huairen and Wei Qingtao had organized, led or participated in criminal groups and committed crimes constituting seven offenses, including intentional homicide and fraud. The courts said the sentences were handed down in accordance with the law, taking into account the facts, nature and circumstances of each defendant's crimes, as well as the degree of harm they caused to society. Since 2023, China and Myanmar have carried out joint operations that led to the dismantling of four major criminal gangs in Myanmar's Kokang region, according to the Criminal Investigation Bureau of the Ministry of Public Security. From October last year to August this year, the number of telecom fraud cases in China declined year-on-year for 11 consecutive months. By the end of 2025, Chinese courts had concluded first-instance trials of more than 27,000 cases related to telecom fraud operations in northern Myanmar, with more than 41,000 repatriated suspects sentenced, according to China's Supreme People's Court, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Huo Zhengxin, a professor at the China University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times that the case falls under Article 8 of China's Criminal Law, which provides for the exercise of protective jurisdiction. The provision states that China's criminal law may apply when foreign nationals commit crimes outside China's territory against the Chinese state or its citizens, provided that the minimum penalty for the offense under Chinese law is a fixed-term prison sentence of at least three years, unless the act is not punishable under the law of the place where it was committed. "Protective jurisdiction is also a widely recognized basis for jurisdiction under international law," Huo said. As crime becomes increasingly transnational, offenses targeting Chinese citizens overseas have become a recurring concern. The Myanmar-based telecom fraud cases serve as a typical example of the extraterritorial application of China's criminal law. They demonstrate China's efforts to protect the personal safety and property rights of its citizens both at home and abroad, while delivering a strong deterrent to transnational organized crime, Huo said. The differentiated sentences handed down by the courts in accordance with China's criminal law also demonstrate that Chinese judicial authorities strictly apply the law and determine penalties based on the degree of culpability of each defendant, he said. Regarding deportation as an additional penalty in the verdicts, Huo noted that the punishment applies only to foreign nationals and stateless persons, and not to Chinese citizens or foreign nationals entitled to diplomatic immunity. Deportation can be imposed either as an independent punishment or as an additional penalty. When imposed as an additional penalty, deportation generally applies to defendants convicted of serious crimes and takes effect after they have completed their principal sentences or been released on parole, with the aim of preventing them from continuing to endanger public safety in China, Huo said.

item.title: The world's first green ammonia ship-to-ship bunkering completed in China's Zhoushan
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 19:05:00
The world's first commercial ship-to-ship green ammonia bunkering operation takes place at an anchorage in Zhoushan, East China's Zhejiang Province, on October 13, 2026. Photo: Courtesy of CEEC The world's first commercial ship-to-ship bunkering of green ammonia at an anchorage has been completed in Zhoushan, East China's Zhejiang Province, marking a major milestone in the country's commercial application of green fuels in international shipping. A total of 1,000 tons of green ammonia produced at China Energy Engineering Corp's (CEEC) Songyuan Hydrogen Energy Industrial Park was supplied to Mineral Europa, an ammonia-powered vessel owned by Belgian maritime group CMB.TECH, through Shenghang Yongle, the world's first dedicated liquid ammonia bunkering vessel. Following the bunkering operation, Mineral Europa is expected to depart from Zhoushan, cross the Pacific Ocean and head to Australia for commercial shipping operations. The operation was described as achieving six world firsts, including the implementation of the world's first take-or-pay sales contract for green ammonia in ocean shipping, the first commercial ship-to-ship green ammonia bunkering operation at an anchorage, and the entry into service of the world's first dedicated ammonia fuel bunkering vessel. Other milestones include the issuance of the world's first ship-to-ship liquid ammonia bunkering license, the realization of full-chain carbon footprint traceability from production facilities to port storage tanks by the world's first green ammonia project directly powered by renewable electricity, and the first commercial ocean voyage by a 210,000-ton ammonia-powered bulk carrier. The bunkering operation was jointly carried out by CEEC Hydrogen Energy Co, Belgian shipping group CMB.TECH and Jiangsu Andefu Energy Technology Co. The successful operation marked the first completion of the entire green ammonia supply chain for marine fuel, covering production, storage, transportation, bunkering and application. It also provides a replicable Chinese solution for the green fuel industry to move beyond individual technology demonstrations toward large-scale commercial operations. All the green ammonia used in the operation came from CEEC's Songyuan Hydrogen Energy Industrial Park, an integrated green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol project developed under the company's Qingqing No.1 initiative. The first phase of the Songyuan project, the world's largest integrated green hydrogen, ammonia and methanol project, officially commenced operations on December 16, 2025. The establishment of a complete supply chain linking Songyuan, Nanjing Port, Zhoushan Port and international ocean shipping routes demonstrates China's capacity to produce green ammonia on a large scale in accordance with international standards and develop cross-regional green energy supply networks. It also highlights the advantages of China's green ammonia industry in terms of environmental credentials, cost competitiveness and a well-developed industrial supply chain. The operation is expected to provide practical experience for the future commissioning of ammonia storage tanks at Panjin Port and the development of a large-scale commercial logistics system capable of supplying green ammonia directly by sea. As the International Maritime Organization's net zero emissions target for shipping draws closer, demand for zero-carbon alternative fuels is increasingly shifting from being driven by policy initiatives to becoming a growing commercial necessity in the global shipping market. Green ammonia can be produced on a large scale using renewable energy sources, including wind, solar and hydropower, together with water and air. The fuel also offers advantages including high volumetric energy density, relatively easy liquefaction and transportation. According to a report seen on the website of Ammonia Energy Association, ammonia would become the dominant fuel choice for new ships by 2042; and it would represent 25 percent of the maritime fuel mix by 2050. item.title: China, South Korea reportedly restart joint patrols in Yellow Sea to curb illegal fishing, signaling improved maritime trust
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 17:07:00
A drone photo taken on Sept. 1, 2026 shows a fishing boat sailing out of a fishing port in Qingdao, East China's Shandong Province. The new fishing season in the Yellow Sea and Bohai Sea kicked off on Tuesday after a four-month summer fishing moratorium. Photo: Xinhua China and South Korea have reportedly resumed joint patrols in the provisional measures zone in the Yellow Sea after a four-year hiatus, with the move showing improved mutual trust and helping promote legal fishing and maritime cooperation, a Chinese expert said. South Korea's Embassy in China said that China and South Korea have been conducting joint patrols starting October 8 to crack down on illegal fishing and other violations in the relevant areas. The patrols, which will continue until October 17, mark the resumption of joint operations after a four-year suspension since 2022, Yonhap News reported on Monday. During the patrols, fisheries guidance and law enforcement officials from the two countries will board each other's vessels to exchange law enforcement methods and experience, while strengthening on-site coordination, according to the report. "Restarting joint law enforcement after four years, with law enforcement personnel from the two sides boarding each other's vessels, is an uncommon practice and reflects to some extent the level of mutual trust between China and South Korea," Lü Chao, a research fellow at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Tuesday. The cooperation is beneficial to promoting legal fishing activities in the Yellow Sea, Lü said, noting that establishing joint law enforcement is "not an easy achievement" and represents a positive development after relations between the two countries improved. A South Korean embassy official in China was also quoted as saying that "one of the areas where cooperation results have emerged since the South Korea-China summit is the crackdown on illegal fishing." The official added that "through this joint patrol, the two countries will further strengthen cooperation and communication between their law enforcement agencies," according to the Yonhap News report. The joint patrols were carried out in accordance with an agreement reached by the two countries to enhance cooperation and eliminate illegal fishing activities. "The Chinese government has always called on Chinese fishermen to conduct fishing activities in accordance with legal rules," Lü said, adding that joint law enforcement could help reduce fishing-related disputes, ensure lawful fishing operations in relevant waters and promote a more institutionalized approach to curbing illegal fishing. Chinese authorities previously carried out a fishing moratorium law enforcement campaign from May 1 to September 16, launching intensive enforcement operations in multiple maritime areas, including waters near the eastern boundary line of the China-South Korea provisional measures zone. The campaign targeted serious violations such as organized illegal fishing, fishing vessels entering closed waters before the official opening of the fishing season, and illegal fishing activities involving high-powered speedboats. At the fourth China-South Korea meeting on maritime affairs dialogue and cooperation, held on September 21, the two sides agreed that maritime affairs are an important component of bilateral relations and pledged to continue working toward building the Yellow Sea into "a sea of peace, friendship and cooperation." The two sides agreed to make better use of maritime dialogue mechanisms, strengthen communication, properly manage differences, advance maritime boundary negotiations, and enhance practical cooperation in areas including defense, law enforcement, fisheries, scientific research, environmental protection, shipping, search and rescue, as well as ocean and polar affairs. Lü said that after South Korea's new administration adopted a more pragmatic approach, the two countries completed reciprocal visits within a few months, and the joint patrols were launched shortly after the maritime cooperation dialogue, which he described as a measure to enhance mutual trust between law enforcement agencies and promote bilateral relations. "Dialogue is necessary. It can help resolve relevant issues and also serve as a precautionary measure to prevent disputes from escalating into serious incidents," Lü added.
